meta.title: What's covered
meta.description: Which intellectual-property and regulatory questions apply to an Ayurvedic product, and how they connect.

heading: Understanding Ayurveda's IP and regulatory landscape
standfirst: Different parts of an Ayurvedic product raise different questions. This page maps which is which.

distinction.heading: Two questions, and why they are joined
distinction.ipBody: How do I secure, or understand, rights in this? It is about exclusivity: what you can stop other people doing, for how long, and in which countries.
distinction.regBody: What must I do before I can make, sell or advertise this? It is about permission: what the state requires of you before a product may reach a buyer.
distinction.couplingHeading: For Ayurveda, they are one question asked twice
distinction.couplingBody: Most industries can treat these separately. Here you cannot, because the regulatory classification of a formulation determines what intellectual property is realistically available to it. A preparation taken unchanged from an authoritative text is documented knowledge, which is why the composition is hard to claim — and the same fact is what lets it use the classical licensing route. Change the formulation and both answers change together.
distinction.matrixHeading: What each product class opens and closes
distinction.matrixNote: Short cells by design. The detail belongs in an answer with the passage attached.

classical_generic.ip: The composition is documented traditional knowledge, so it is not realistically claimable. Brand, packaging and artwork remain available.
classical_generic.regulatory: The classical route, resting on the authoritative texts the drug rules recognise.
classical_generic.abs: Duties can still attach to the biological resource used, whatever the formulation's status.

patent_proprietary.ip: Arguable on what was actually changed. The classical base stands as prior art against the rest of it.
patent_proprietary.regulatory: Licensed as a patent or proprietary medicine, with conditions of its own.
patent_proprietary.abs: Duties attach, and they begin to interact with anything you file.

new_non_classical_drug.ip: The widest room. A novel process or a combination doing something previously unknown can be claimed on its own merits.
new_non_classical_drug.regulatory: The new-drug route, which asks for evidence rather than textual authority.
new_non_classical_drug.abs: Duties attach, and disclosure of the biological source becomes part of the filing.

phytopharmaceutical.ip: A purified or standardised fraction is the most patentable form this product takes, because it is furthest from the whole-plant preparation.
phytopharmaceutical.regulatory: A route of its own, with data requirements separate from both the classical and the new-drug paths.
phytopharmaceutical.abs: Duties attach; the resource is usually a named plant, which makes the trigger easy to identify and hard to avoid.

ayurveda_aahar.ip: Brand, packaging and design. A food cannot be claimed as a medicine, and the composition is rarely claimable.
ayurveda_aahar.regulatory: The food route, under the food authority rather than the drug regulator.
ayurveda_aahar.abs: Duties can attach to the resource. Being a food does not remove them.

cosmetic.ip: Brand, packaging and the design of the article. Composition claims are narrow.
cosmetic.regulatory: The cosmetic route, which turns on external use for appearance rather than therapeutic effect.
cosmetic.abs: Duties can attach to the resource, on the same basis as any other use.

rights.heading: The rights, one at a time
rights.standfirst: Each of these answers a different question. Reading them as interchangeable is the most common way an Ayurvedic business spends money on the wrong protection.

labels.inAyurveda: How it shows up in Ayurveda
labels.question: A question people actually ask

patents.title: Patents
patents.protects: A new invention that is not obvious to someone skilled in the field, for a limited term, in exchange for disclosing how it works.
patents.inAyurveda: Rarely the formulation itself. More often a process, a delivery form, a purified fraction, or a specific combination that does something the individual ingredients were not already known to do.
patents.question: We reformulated a classical preparation — is there anything patentable in it?
patents.doesNot: It does not give you permission to sell. A granted patent and a manufacturing licence are separate things and neither implies the other. It also does not make a formulation new: documented traditional knowledge is prior art, and an aggregation of properties already known is generally not an invention.
patents.jurisdiction: India, with separate filings in every other country you want protection in.

gi.title: Geographical indications
gi.protects: A name identifying goods as coming from a particular place, where a quality, reputation or characteristic is due to that origin.
gi.inAyurveda: Regional herbs and preparations whose character is tied to where they grow, or to how a locality has long made them.
gi.question: Our herb grows only in one district — does that qualify for a geographical indication?
gi.doesNot: It is not owned by one company. A GI is held for a class of producers who meet the specification, so registering one does not give you exclusivity over your competitors in the same region. It also does not stop anyone outside the region making a similar product under a different name.
gi.jurisdiction: India. Protection elsewhere is separate and works differently from country to country.

trademarks.title: Trademarks
trademarks.protects: A sign that tells a buyer who made the product.
trademarks.inAyurveda: Brand names for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani products, house marks, and the get-up of a pack.
trademarks.question: Can we register our brand name if it contains a classical formulation name?
trademarks.doesNot: It does not hand you a classical formulation name. A mark that merely describes what the product is will struggle, and other manufacturers need to use the same classical name for the same preparation. Registration also does not license a claim that the advertising rules prohibit — the mark and the claim are judged separately.
trademarks.jurisdiction: India, with separate registration abroad or through an international filing system.

copyright.title: Copyright
copyright.protects: Original expression — text, images, artwork, software — not the ideas, facts or methods inside it.
copyright.inAyurveda: Course material, translations and commentaries, packaging artwork, photography, software. The classical texts themselves are long out of copyright; a new translation or an original commentary is a new work with its own term.
copyright.question: Can we stop someone copying our training material?
copyright.doesNot: It does not protect a formulation, a process, or a treatment protocol. Someone may read your book and make your product.
copyright.jurisdiction: India, with protection in most other countries arising automatically under treaty rather than by registration.

designs.title: Designs
designs.protects: How a manufactured article looks — its shape, configuration, pattern or ornament.
designs.inAyurveda: A bottle, a dispenser, a jar closure, the form of a pack.
designs.question: We designed a distinctive dispenser — can we protect the shape?
designs.doesNot: It does not protect how the article works, and it does not survive publication: showing the design before you apply can destroy the right you were about to register.
designs.jurisdiction: India, with separate filings or an international route abroad.

plantVariety.title: Plant variety rights
plantVariety.protects: A new plant variety that is distinct from what exists, uniform within itself, and stable across generations.
plantVariety.inAyurveda: Cultivated varieties of medicinal plants developed for yield, potency, or hardiness.
plantVariety.question: We developed a cultivar of a medicinal plant — can we register it?
plantVariety.doesNot: It is not a patent on the plant, and it sits alongside farmers' rights rather than overriding them.
plantVariety.jurisdiction: India, under a regime of its own rather than under the patent system.

tradeSecrets.title: Trade secrets
tradeSecrets.protects: In India, no standalone statute. Confidential information is held through contract, employment terms and the general law rather than by any registration.
tradeSecrets.inAyurveda: Process know-how, sourcing relationships, standardisation methods — precisely the things a patent application would have to disclose.
tradeSecrets.question: Should we file a patent or keep the process confidential?
tradeSecrets.doesNot: It gives you nothing against independent discovery or reverse engineering. And it is in direct tension with two disclosure obligations: what a patent application must reveal, and what a regulatory dossier must contain. Choosing secrecy is choosing to forgo both.
tradeSecrets.jurisdiction: India — and the absence of a dedicated statute is itself the point, so this section states a gap rather than a regime.

tk.title: Traditional knowledge
tk.protects: It depends on whether the knowledge is codified in published texts or held by a community. These are different problems with different answers.
tk.inAyurveda: Codified knowledge in the authoritative texts is the reason many formulation patents fail — it is prior art, and it is documented specifically so that it can be cited as such. Community-held knowledge raises a different question, about consent and about sharing what comes of it.
tk.question: Our formulation comes from a community's practice — what do we owe them?
tk.doesNot: Defensive protection stops others from patenting what is already known. It does not give you an exclusive right of your own, and it is not a substitute for the access and benefit-sharing duties below.
tk.jurisdiction: India, and internationally: a 2024 treaty addresses intellectual property, genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, including what an applicant must disclose.

regulation.heading: What is required before you can sell
regulation.standfirst: Classification comes first, because it decides which of the rest apply to you.

classification.title: Product classification
classification.body: Everything downstream follows from what your product is: a classical preparation, a patent or proprietary medicine, a new non-classical drug, a phytopharmaceutical, a food, or a cosmetic. The classification is not a label you choose — it follows from the formulation, the claim you make, and how far you have moved from an authoritative text.
classification.watchFor: Businesses often decide their route first and describe the product to fit. That is the wrong way round, and it is expensive to unwind.

licence.title: Manufacturing licence
licence.body: Making an Ayurvedic drug for sale requires a licence from the state licensing authority, and the licence is specific to what you make and where you make it.
licence.watchFor: A licence covering classical preparations does not automatically cover a proprietary medicine. Changing the formulation can put you outside the licence you already hold.

gmp.title: Manufacturing practice
gmp.body: Good manufacturing practice requirements for these products cover premises, equipment, staff, water, in-process checks and record-keeping. They are a condition of the licence rather than an optional standard.
gmp.watchFor: Contract manufacturing does not transfer the obligation away from the brand owner.

quality.title: Quality and pharmacopoeial standards
quality.body: Published pharmacopoeial monographs set identity, purity and strength standards for many single drugs and formulations, and a formulary records recognised preparations.
quality.watchFor: Where a monograph exists, meeting it is not a marketing claim you can make — it is the baseline. Where none exists, you have to be able to say what standard you are working to and why.

labelling.title: Labelling
labelling.body: What must appear on the pack is set by more than one regime at once: drug rules, packaged-commodity rules, and — if the product is a food — the food authority's labelling regulations.
labelling.watchFor: The regimes overlap rather than nest. Satisfying one does not mean you have satisfied another.

advertising.title: Advertising and claims
advertising.body: Advertising of these products is restricted, and certain disease claims are prohibited outright rather than merely regulated. The restriction applies to the advertisement, not only to the label.
advertising.watchFor: A claim that is prohibited on a pack is generally prohibited in a social media post as well. Enforcement follows the claim, not the medium.

food.title: The food and nutraceutical route
food.body: A product intended as a food or supplement rather than a medicine falls under the food authority, which has its own category for Ayurveda-derived foods, its own approval process, and its own limits on what a claim may say.
food.watchFor: This route is often chosen to avoid drug licensing. It brings different obligations rather than fewer, and it narrows what you may claim the product does.

cosmetic.title: The cosmetic route
cosmetic.body: A preparation applied externally for appearance rather than therapeutic effect is regulated as a cosmetic, with its own registration and labelling requirements.
cosmetic.watchFor: The boundary is the claim. The same cream is a cosmetic or a drug depending on what you say it does.

clinicalEvidence.title: Evidence for a new drug
clinicalEvidence.body: A formulation outside the classical texts, or one making a new therapeutic claim, moves into territory where safety and effectiveness have to be shown rather than inferred from tradition.
clinicalEvidence.watchFor: Traditional use can support some routes and not others. Which one you are on decides whether it counts.

marketAccess.title: Import, export and market access
marketAccess.body: An Indian licence carries no weight abroad. Each destination decides for itself whether your product is a medicine, a supplement, a food or a novel ingredient, and answers that question by its own rules.
marketAccess.watchFor: The most common surprise is that the product changes category at the border, and with it the entire compliance burden.

abs.heading: Access and benefit sharing
abs.standfirst: This is the obligation most often discovered late, and it is the one that touches both halves of this page: it can attach to your manufacturing and to your patent application at the same time.
abs.whoBody: The obligations differ depending on who you are. Indian individuals and companies, foreign entities, registered practitioners and researchers are not treated identically, and the difference is not a formality — it changes which authority you deal with and what you must do before you begin.
abs.triggerBody: The trigger is accessing a biological resource, or knowledge associated with it, for research or for commercial use. Wild collection, cultivation on someone else's terms, and sourcing through a trader are not the same act, and they are not treated the same way.
abs.authorityBody: There is a national authority and there are state boards, and which one you approach depends on who you are and what you are doing. Approaching the wrong one costs time rather than being fatal, but it is avoidable.
abs.sharingBody: Benefit sharing is not always a payment. It can be monetary, or take the form of technology transfer, joint ownership, local employment, or support for conservation — and it is agreed rather than assessed unilaterally.
abs.patentHeading: Where it meets a patent application
abs.patentBody: A patent application drawing on a biological resource carries disclosure obligations about the source, and the two regimes are connected by design rather than by accident. Filing without having addressed access is the most common way this obligation becomes visible — at the point where it is most expensive.
abs.changeBody: The Indian regime was amended, and the rules under it remade, within the last few years. Some categories of user were treated differently after that change than before it. Any statement about who owes what is therefore only as good as its effective date, which is why this product carries one on every answer.
